questions.question: What is the difference between a transition and a keyframe animation?
questions.answer: A transition interpolates between two states triggered by a change (hover/class). A keyframe animation defines multiple steps and can run automatically, loop, alternate, and persist its end state.

questions.question: What does animation-fill-mode: both do?
questions.answer: It applies the first keyframe during the delay (backwards) and keeps the last keyframe after the animation ends (forwards), so the element does not snap back to its pre-animation state.

questions.question: Explain animation-direction values.
questions.answer: normal plays forward, reverse plays backward, alternate alternates forward/backward each cycle, and alternate-reverse starts backward then alternates.

questions.question: How do you run two animations on one element?
questions.answer: Comma-separate them in the animation shorthand (or longhands), each with its own name, duration, easing, and iteration count. Both run simultaneously.

questions.question: How should prefers-reduced-motion be handled for animations?
questions.answer: Disable or drastically shorten decorative animations and transitions, keep essential state changes, disable smooth scrolling, and avoid infinite/large motion for users who request reduced motion.

questions.question: Create a fade-up entrance that keeps its final state.
Why does an entrance animation snap back when it finishes?
questions.answer: The default fill-mode is none, so after the animation the element returns to its underlying styles. Use animation-fill-mode: forwards or both to retain the last keyframe.

questions.question: Why is an infinite animation on a full-page background a performance risk?
questions.answer: It forces continuous painting/compositing and can drain battery, especially on large areas or layout-affecting properties. Keep infinite motion small, transform/opacity-based, and pause when offscreen.
